content.intro: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a common condition that affects many men at some point in their lives. It is defined as the consistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. While it can be a source of significant distress and anxiety, it is important to understand that ED is a medical condition, not a personal failure. It is highly treatable, and seeking help is a positive step toward improving your quality of life and overall health. This lesson will help you understand what ED is, how common it is, and why it matters beyond just sexual health.

sections.heading: Understanding the Basics of ED
sections.text: To understand erectile dysfunction, it helps to think of an erection like a hydraulic system. For an erection to occur, blood must flow into the penis and stay there. This process involves a complex interaction between your brain, nerves, hormones, blood vessels, and muscles. When you are sexually stimulated, your brain sends signals to the nerves in your penis. These nerves release chemicals that tell the muscles in the penile arteries to relax. When these muscles relax, blood flows into the spongy tissue of the penis, causing it to expand and become firm. At the same time, other muscles compress the veins that normally drain blood from the penis, trapping the blood inside and maintaining the erection. Erectile dysfunction occurs when any part of this intricate system fails to work correctly. It is not just about 'not getting hard'; it is about the disruption of this biological sequence. It can be caused by physical issues, such as blocked blood vessels or nerve damage, or psychological factors, such as stress or anxiety. Understanding that this is a mechanical and biological process helps remove the stigma and shame often associated with the condition. It is a health signal, much like chest pain is a signal for heart issues, indicating that something in your body needs attention.

sections.heading: How Common Is It?
sections.text: Erectile dysfunction is far more common than many men realize, which means you are not alone. Statistics show that ED affects approximately 30 million men in the United States alone, and globally, it affects hundreds of millions of men. The prevalence increases with age. For men in their 40s, about 40% experience some degree of ED. By age 50, this number rises to 50%, and by age 70, it affects about 70% of men. However, ED is not exclusively a disease of aging. It can affect men of all ages, including younger men in their 20s and 30s, often due to psychological factors or lifestyle choices. The good news is that because it is so common, there is a vast amount of research and effective treatments available. Many men hesitate to discuss ED with their doctors due to embarrassment, but healthcare providers are trained to handle these conversations with professionalism and empathy. Recognizing the high prevalence of ED can help normalize the experience and encourage men to seek the help they need without delay.

sections.heading: Why It Matters: The Health Connection
sections.text: One of the most important aspects of understanding erectile dysfunction is recognizing its connection to overall health. ED is often an early warning sign of other serious medical conditions, particularly cardiovascular disease. The blood vessels in the penis are much smaller than those in the heart. Therefore, if these small vessels are damaged or narrowed due to plaque buildup (atherosclerosis), it may show up as ED before it causes heart problems. Studies suggest that men with ED are at a higher risk of developing heart disease, stroke, and high blood pressure in the future. Additionally, ED can be linked to diabetes, high cholesterol, and hormonal imbalances. By addressing ED, you are not just improving your sexual health; you are potentially uncovering and treating underlying health issues that could affect your longevity and quality of life. Think of ED as a 'canary in the coal mine' for your vascular health. It is a signal to take a closer look at your overall well-being, including your diet, exercise habits, and heart health. This perspective shifts the focus from a purely sexual problem to a holistic health opportunity.

content.clinical_pearl: Erectile dysfunction is often the first sign of cardiovascular disease. Because the arteries in the penis are smaller than those in the heart, blockages may appear there first. If you have ED, it is crucial to have your heart health evaluated, including blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar levels, to prevent future heart attacks or strokes.
key_points: ED is a common medical condition affecting millions of men, not a personal failure.
It involves a complex interaction of blood flow, nerves, and hormones.
Prevalence increases with age but can affect men of all ages.
ED is often an early warning sign of heart disease and diabetes.
Seeking treatment for ED can improve overall health and quality of life.
Open communication with your doctor is the first step to effective management.

content.intro: Understanding the causes of erectile dysfunction is key to finding the right treatment. ED is rarely caused by a single factor; instead, it is often the result of a combination of physical and psychological issues. In this lesson, we will explore the various risk factors that contribute to ED, distinguishing between those you can change (modifiable) and those you cannot (non-modifiable). By identifying your specific risk factors, you can work with your healthcare provider to create a personalized plan to manage and potentially reverse the condition. Remember, knowing the cause is the first step toward a solution.

sections.heading: Physical Causes: The Body's Role
sections.text: Physical causes are the most common reasons for erectile dysfunction, especially in older men. These issues interfere with the blood flow, nerve signals, or hormonal balance needed for an erection. Cardiovascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries), high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, can restrict blood flow to the penis. Diabetes is a major risk factor, as high blood sugar can damage both the blood vessels and the nerves that control erections. Neurological conditions, such as multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, or spinal cord injuries, can disrupt the nerve signals between the brain and the penis. Hormonal imbalances, particularly low testosterone levels, can also contribute to ED by reducing sexual desire and affecting the physiological processes of erection. Additionally, certain medications, such as those for high blood pressure, depression, or prostate issues, can have ED as a side effect. Understanding these physical links helps in targeting the root cause rather than just the symptom.

sections.heading: Psychological Causes: The Mind's Role
sections.text: The mind plays a crucial role in sexual function. Psychological factors can cause ED by interfering with the brain's ability to send the necessary signals for an erection. Stress, anxiety, and depression are common culprits. Performance anxiety, a fear of not being able to perform sexually, can create a cycle of worry that makes ED worse. Relationship problems, such as poor communication or unresolved conflicts with a partner, can also lead to ED. Mental health issues, such as depression, can reduce libido and make it difficult to become aroused. It is important to recognize that psychological ED is real and valid. It is not 'just in your head' in the sense that it is imaginary; rather, the mind is actively blocking the physical response. Therapy, counseling, and stress management techniques can be highly effective in treating psychologically induced ED. Often, a combination of physical and psychological factors is at play, requiring a holistic approach to treatment.

sections.heading: Lifestyle and Modifiable Risk Factors
sections.text: Many risk factors for ED are related to lifestyle choices, which means they can be changed or managed. Smoking is a major risk factor, as it damages blood vessels and reduces blood flow. Alcohol consumption, especially in excess, can interfere with nerve function and hormone levels. Drug use, particularly illicit drugs, can also cause ED. Obesity is another significant factor, as excess weight is linked to diabetes, heart disease, and low testosterone. A sedentary lifestyle, lacking regular physical activity, contributes to poor cardiovascular health and increases the risk of ED. Diet also plays a role; a diet high in saturated fats, sugars, and processed foods can lead to vascular problems. On the other hand, adopting a healthy lifestyle can significantly improve or even reverse ED. Quitting smoking, reducing alcohol intake, losing weight, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet are powerful tools in managing ED. These changes not only help with sexual function but also improve overall health and longevity.

content.clinical_pearl: Smoking is one of the most significant modifiable risk factors for ED. The chemicals in cigarettes damage the lining of blood vessels, reducing their ability to dilate and allow blood flow. Quitting smoking can improve erectile function within weeks to months, making it one of the most effective lifestyle changes for treating ED.
key_points: Physical causes include heart disease, diabetes, and nerve damage.
Psychological factors like stress and anxiety can block erection signals.
Medications for other conditions can sometimes cause ED as a side effect.
Smoking, alcohol, and drug use significantly increase the risk of ED.
Obesity and a sedentary lifestyle are major modifiable risk factors.
Improving lifestyle habits can often reverse or improve ED symptoms.

lessons.title: Symptoms and How the Disease Develops

content.intro: Recognizing the symptoms of erectile dysfunction is the first step toward getting help. ED can manifest in different ways, from occasional difficulty achieving an erection to a complete inability to maintain one. In this lesson, we will discuss the early warning signs, how the condition progresses over time, and what patients typically experience. We will also cover when to seek urgent care, although ED itself is rarely a medical emergency. Understanding these symptoms can help you communicate more effectively with your healthcare provider and identify the best time to seek treatment.

sections.heading: Early Warning Signs
sections.text: The early signs of erectile dysfunction can be subtle and may come and go. You might notice that it takes longer to get an erection than it used to, or that your erections are not as firm as they were in the past. You may find that you need more direct stimulation to become aroused. Another early sign is the inability to maintain an erection throughout sexual activity. These symptoms might occur occasionally and then disappear, which can lead to confusion and anxiety. It is important to pay attention to these changes, even if they seem minor. Occasional ED is normal and can be caused by stress, fatigue, or alcohol. However, if these symptoms persist for more than a few weeks or become more frequent, it is a sign that something may be wrong. Early intervention can prevent the condition from worsening and make treatment more effective. Do not wait for the problem to become severe before seeking help.

sections.heading: How the Disease Progresses
sections.text: Erectile dysfunction can progress gradually or suddenly, depending on the underlying cause. In cases related to physical health issues, such as diabetes or heart disease, the progression is often slow. Over time, the damage to blood vessels or nerves worsens, making it increasingly difficult to achieve or maintain an erection. In cases related to psychological factors, the progression can be more rapid and cyclical. A single episode of ED can lead to anxiety about future performance, which in turn causes more ED. This 'vicious cycle' can make the condition feel overwhelming and unmanageable. In some cases, ED can become complete, meaning no erections are possible, even during sleep or masturbation. This is a sign that the underlying cause is significant and requires medical attention. Understanding the progression of ED helps in setting realistic expectations for treatment and recovery. It also highlights the importance of addressing the root cause early on.

sections.heading: What Patients Actually Feel
sections.text: Beyond the physical symptoms, ED can have a profound emotional impact. Many men feel frustrated, embarrassed, or inadequate. The loss of sexual function can affect self-esteem and confidence, not just in the bedroom but in other areas of life. It can strain relationships with partners, leading to misunderstandings and conflict. Some men may withdraw from social situations or avoid intimacy altogether. It is important to recognize that these feelings are normal and valid. ED is a medical condition, not a reflection of your masculinity or worth. Open communication with your partner can help alleviate some of the emotional burden. Many partners are supportive and willing to work together to find a solution. Seeking professional help, whether from a doctor or a therapist, can provide the tools and support needed to cope with the emotional aspects of ED. Remember, you are not alone, and help is available.

content.clinical_pearl: Nocturnal erections, or erections during sleep, are a key diagnostic clue. If you still experience erections during sleep or upon waking, it suggests that the physical mechanisms for erection are intact, and the cause may be psychological. If you do not experience nocturnal erections, it may indicate a physical cause, such as nerve or blood vessel damage.
key_points: Early signs include difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection.
ED can progress gradually due to physical causes or rapidly due to anxiety.
Emotional impacts include frustration, embarrassment, and relationship strain.
Occasional ED is normal, but persistent symptoms require medical attention.
Nocturnal erections can help distinguish between physical and psychological causes.
Open communication with your partner and doctor is essential for management.

content.intro: Getting a diagnosis for erectile dysfunction (ED) can feel intimidating, but it is a routine and straightforward process. Think of your doctor as a detective trying to solve a puzzle. They need to figure out if the cause is physical, psychological, or a mix of both. This distinction is crucial because the treatment for a blood flow issue is very different from the treatment for stress or anxiety. The good news is that modern medicine has many tools to help identify the root cause quickly and accurately. You do not need to feel embarrassed; doctors hear about this every day, and their only goal is to help you regain your confidence and health. This lesson will walk you through exactly what to expect, from the initial conversation to any tests that might be needed, so you can walk into your appointment feeling prepared and calm.

sections.heading: The Initial Consultation: Your Story Matters
sections.text: The most important part of diagnosing ED is the conversation you have with your doctor. This is not just a quick check-up; it is a detailed interview. Your doctor will ask about your medical history, your current medications, and your lifestyle habits. They may ask sensitive questions about your sexual history, your relationship status, and your mental health. It is vital to be honest and open. For example, if you are stressed at work, if you are smoking, or if you have trouble getting an erection in the morning but not with a partner, these details help the doctor distinguish between physical and psychological causes. If you have morning erections, it often suggests that the physical machinery is working, and the issue might be related to anxiety or performance pressure. Your doctor will also review any other health conditions you have, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease, as these are closely linked to ED. They may use a standardized questionnaire, such as the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF), to quantify the severity of your symptoms. This helps track your progress over time. Remember, there are no 'wrong' answers. The more information you provide, the better your doctor can tailor a treatment plan specifically for you. Do not hide your use of recreational drugs or alcohol, as these can significantly impact erectile function. This conversation is the foundation of your care, so take your time and share what you are comfortable with.

sections.heading: Physical Examination and Basic Health Checks
sections.text: After the conversation, your doctor will likely perform a physical examination. This is a standard medical procedure designed to check for physical signs that might explain your symptoms. The doctor will check your blood pressure, heart rate, and listen to your heart and lungs. They will examine your genitals to look for any physical abnormalities, such as scar tissue from previous injuries or surgery, or signs of hormonal imbalance like low testosterone (which might present as reduced body hair or breast tissue growth). They will also check the nerves in your groin area by testing sensation. Additionally, your doctor will likely order blood tests. These tests are crucial because ED can be an early warning sign of cardiovascular disease. The blood work typically includes a check of your blood sugar levels (to screen for diabetes), cholesterol levels (to assess heart health), and testosterone levels. Low testosterone can cause low libido and ED, but it is not the most common cause. The doctor is looking for 'silent' killers like high blood pressure or high cholesterol that damage blood vessels over time. If your blood vessels are narrowed due to plaque buildup, it is harder for blood to flow into the penis. This is why ED is sometimes called the 'canary in the coal mine' for heart health. If your blood tests show abnormalities, your doctor may refer you to a cardiologist or endocrinologist for further management. This step ensures that we are treating the whole person, not just the symptom.

sections.heading: Advanced Testing: When Is It Needed?
sections.text: For most men, the diagnosis is made based on history, physical exam, and basic blood tests. However, in complex cases, or if first-line treatments fail, your doctor might recommend advanced testing. One such test is the Nocturnal Penile Tumescence (NPT) test. This involves wearing a small device on your penis while you sleep to measure erections. Since healthy men have erections during REM sleep, this test helps determine if the cause is physical (no erections during sleep) or psychological (erections occur during sleep but not during sex). Another test is a penile Doppler ultrasound. This is a painless procedure where a small amount of medication is injected into the penis to induce an erection, and then an ultrasound machine is used to visualize blood flow. This helps identify if there is a blockage in the arteries or a leak in the veins (venous leak). These tests are not routine and are usually reserved for cases where surgery or specialized therapy is being considered. It is important to know that you do not need to undergo invasive procedures to get help. Most men respond well to oral medications, which are prescribed based on the initial assessment. If your doctor suggests advanced testing, ask them to explain why it is necessary for your specific case. Understanding the purpose of each test can reduce anxiety and help you feel more in control of the diagnostic process.

content.clinical_pearl: Erectile dysfunction is often the first sign of cardiovascular disease. The blood vessels in the penis are smaller than those in the heart, so they show damage earlier. If you have ED, it is crucial to have your heart health checked, even if you feel fine otherwise. Treating ED can also improve your overall vascular health.
key_points: Honesty with your doctor is the most important step in getting an accurate diagnosis.
Morning erections often suggest a psychological rather than physical cause.
Blood tests for diabetes, cholesterol, and testosterone are standard and essential.
Physical exams check for hormonal signs and nerve function.
Advanced tests like ultrasound are only needed in complex or treatment-resistant cases.
ED can be an early warning sign of heart disease, so cardiovascular health is key.

content.intro: Once the cause of your erectile dysfunction is identified, there are many effective treatments available. It is important to remember that ED is highly treatable, and most men find a solution that works for them. The choice of treatment depends on the underlying cause, your overall health, your preferences, and your partner’s preferences. There is no 'one size fits all' approach. Some men prefer oral medications, while others may benefit from lifestyle changes, therapy, or devices. This lesson will explore the full range of options, from simple lifestyle adjustments to advanced surgical procedures. We will explain how each treatment works in plain language, discuss potential side effects, and help you understand how to choose the best path for you. The goal is not just to achieve an erection, but to restore your confidence and intimacy. Let’s look at the tools available to help you get there.

sections.heading: Oral Medications: The First Line of Defense
sections.text: For most men, the first step in treatment is oral medication. These drugs, known as PDE5 inhibitors, include sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil (Levitra), and avanafil (Stendra). They work by enhancing the effects of nitric oxide, a chemical your body produces to relax muscles in the penis and increase blood flow. Think of them as a 'volume knob' for blood flow. They do not cause an erection on their own; you still need sexual stimulation. Sildenafil and vardenafil typically last 4-5 hours, while tadalafil can last up to 36 hours, allowing for more spontaneity. Avanafil works faster, often within 15-30 minutes. These medications are generally safe and effective for the majority of men. However, they are not suitable for everyone. Men taking nitrates for chest pain (angina) should never take PDE5 inhibitors, as the combination can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. Common side effects include headache, flushing, indigestion, and nasal congestion. These are usually mild and go away quickly. If one medication does not work or causes side effects, your doctor can switch you to another. It is important to take these medications as directed, usually on an empty stomach for best results (except for tadalafil, which is less affected by food). Do not exceed the recommended dose, as this does not improve effectiveness but increases the risk of side effects.

sections.heading: Non-Oral Treatments: Devices and Injections
sections.text: If oral medications are not effective or are contraindicated, there are other options. Vacuum Erection Devices (VEDs) are non-invasive pumps that create a vacuum around the penis, drawing blood into it. A tension ring is then placed at the base to keep the blood in. This can be a good option for men who want to avoid medication or have had surgery. It requires some practice to use correctly, but it is safe and effective. Another option is intracavernosal injection therapy. This involves injecting a small amount of medication directly into the side of the penis using a very fine needle. The medication relaxes the smooth muscle and increases blood flow, causing an erection within 5-10 minutes. While the idea of an injection may seem daunting, most men find it easy to learn and painless. The risk of priapism (an erection lasting more than 4 hours) is low but serious, so you must be trained on how to use it correctly. Urethral suppositories are another option, where a small pellet is inserted into the urethra. This is less common due to discomfort and lower efficacy. For men with low testosterone, hormone replacement therapy may be considered, but only if blood tests confirm low levels. It is important to discuss the risks and benefits of testosterone therapy with your doctor, as it is not a cure for ED on its own and may have side effects like increased red blood cell count or prostate issues.

sections.heading: Surgery and Psychological Support
sections.text: For men who do not respond to other treatments, penile implants are a highly effective surgical option. An implant consists of inflatable or malleable rods placed inside the penis. Inflatable implants allow you to control when you have an erection by pumping fluid from a reservoir in your abdomen into the rods. This provides a natural-looking and feeling erection. Surgery is usually outpatient and has a high satisfaction rate. It is considered a last resort because it is irreversible, but for many men, it restores their sexual life completely. In addition to physical treatments, psychological support is crucial if anxiety, depression, or relationship issues are contributing to ED. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and sex therapy can help you address performance anxiety, improve communication with your partner, and develop healthier attitudes towards sex. Often, a combination of physical and psychological treatments yields the best results. For example, taking a PDE5 inhibitor while undergoing therapy can help break the cycle of anxiety and failure. It is important to involve your partner in the treatment process if possible. Their support and understanding can make a significant difference in your recovery. Remember, ED is a medical condition, not a reflection of your masculinity or desirability. Seeking help is a sign of strength and care for your well-being.

content.clinical_pearl: PDE5 inhibitors do not cause erections without sexual stimulation. They enhance the natural response. If you are not aroused, the medication will not work. This is why mental relaxation and intimacy are just as important as the pill itself. Communication with your partner is a key part of the treatment.
key_points: Oral medications like Viagra and Cialis are effective for most men but require sexual stimulation.
Never take PDE5 inhibitors if you are taking nitrates for heart conditions.
Vacuum devices and injections are effective alternatives if pills do not work.
Penile implants are a highly successful surgical option for refractory cases.
Psychological therapy is essential if anxiety or relationship issues are involved.
Involve your partner in the treatment process for better outcomes.

content.intro: While erectile dysfunction can be treated, preventing it or slowing its progression is equally important. Many causes of ED are linked to lifestyle factors that you can control. By making healthy choices, you can protect your vascular health, which is essential for erectile function. This lesson combines prevention strategies with tips for living well with ED. We will discuss how to avoid getting ED in the first place, how to prevent complications if you already have it, and how to maintain a fulfilling sex life. Prevention is not just about avoiding ED; it is about improving your overall health and longevity. Small changes in your diet, exercise, and stress management can have a big impact. Let’s explore how to take charge of your health and enjoy a vibrant, active life.

sections.heading: Primary Prevention: Lifestyle Changes That Protect You
sections.text: The best way to prevent erectile dysfunction is to take care of your heart and blood vessels. Since ED is often a sign of vascular disease, what is good for your heart is good for your penis. Start by quitting smoking. Smoking damages blood vessels and reduces blood flow, which is a major cause of ED. If you smoke, seek help to quit; even reducing smoking can help. Maintain a healthy weight. Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, is linked to lower testosterone and higher inflammation, both of which contribute to ED. Aim for a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 18.5 and 24.9. Exercise regularly. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling. Exercise improves blood flow, reduces stress, and boosts testosterone. Strength training twice a week can also help. Eat a heart-healthy diet. Focus on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats (like olive oil and nuts). The Mediterranean diet is particularly beneficial. Limit processed foods, sugar, and saturated fats. Manage stress and sleep well. Chronic stress raises cortisol levels, which can lower testosterone and impair sexual function. Aim for 7-9 hours of quality sleep per night. Poor sleep is linked to lower testosterone and higher stress. Limit alcohol consumption. While moderate alcohol may not harm, excessive drinking can cause ED. By adopting these habits, you not only reduce your risk of ED but also lower your risk of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes.

sections.heading: Secondary Prevention: Managing ED and Preventing Complications
sections.text: If you already have ED, the goal is to prevent it from worsening and to manage any underlying conditions. Regular monitoring of your blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol is essential. Work with your doctor to keep these numbers in the target range. For example, aim for a blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg and an HbA1c below 7% if you have diabetes. Adhere to your treatment plan. Whether it is medication, therapy, or lifestyle changes, consistency is key. Do not stop treatment because you feel better; ED is a chronic condition that requires ongoing management. Monitor for side effects of your medications and report them to your doctor. If you are using a vacuum device, follow the instructions carefully to avoid injury. If you are on testosterone therapy, regular blood tests are needed to monitor hormone levels and red blood cell count. Be aware of the risk of priapism with injections or suppositories. If an erection lasts more than 4 hours, seek emergency medical care immediately to prevent permanent damage. Regular check-ups with your urologist and primary care physician are important to adjust your treatment as needed. ED can be a marker for other health issues, so staying on top of your overall health is crucial. Do not ignore new symptoms or changes in your condition. Early intervention can prevent complications and improve your quality of life.

sections.heading: Living Well: Intimacy, Communication, and Mental Health
sections.text: Living well with ED involves more than just physical treatment; it is about maintaining intimacy and emotional well-being. Open communication with your partner is vital. Share your feelings, fears, and desires. Involve your partner in your treatment journey. This can strengthen your bond and reduce performance pressure. Explore different forms of intimacy. Sex is not just about penetration. Focus on emotional connection, foreplay, and mutual pleasure. This can reduce anxiety and make sexual experiences more enjoyable. Consider seeking support from a therapist or counselor if you are struggling with anxiety, depression, or relationship issues. Mental health is closely linked to sexual health. Joining a support group can also be helpful. Talking to others who are going through similar experiences can reduce feelings of isolation and provide practical tips. Practice self-compassion. ED is a medical condition, not a personal failure. Be patient with yourself and your partner. Recovery may take time, and there may be setbacks. Celebrate small victories. Finally, stay active and engaged in life. Pursue hobbies, spend time with friends and family, and maintain a positive outlook. A fulfilling life outside the bedroom contributes to a healthy sex life. Remember, you are not alone, and help is available. By taking a holistic approach to your health, you can live a happy, healthy, and intimate life despite ED.

content.clinical_pearl: ED is a window into your vascular health. Preventing ED is essentially preventing heart disease. The same lifestyle changes that improve erections—quitting smoking, exercising, eating well—also protect your heart, brain, and overall longevity. Treat your body as a whole system.
key_points: Quit smoking and maintain a healthy weight to protect blood vessels.
Exercise 150 minutes per week and eat a Mediterranean-style diet.
Manage stress and prioritize 7-9 hours of sleep per night.
Monitor blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol regularly.
Communicate openly with your partner to reduce performance anxiety.
Seek mental health support if needed; ED is a medical, not moral, issue.
